chapter_theme: Under the heading அமைச்சர், eight verses on the king's counsellors: the royal assembly shows their learning, the king's faults are laid on those who shaped him, a king without many counsellors for eyes is helpless in trouble, the king should test and hold the wise, restrained guardians keep his life, good ministers press unwelcome good on him, the wise may even beguile him at the right moment, and the experienced take care never to provoke his anger.

258.reading: The council of the king of killing anger shows a man's breadth of learning and the skill of his set speech, just as the cool flood that pours down in full at the river's head shows how much rain fell on the mountain.
258.nuance: The argument runs from effect to hidden cause: the rain on the mountain is not seen, only the flood below, and the learning stored in a man is not seen until the king's assembly draws it out. துணை here is a measure, how much, not a companion. The king is கொல்சின, of killing anger, so the assembly that tests is also a dangerous one.
258.domain_note: the king's counsellor before the royal assembly

pazhamozhi.literal: the flood shows the measure of the rain on the mountain

story.act: no story; the river in spate is the instance

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a counsellor's learning and eloquence are known by what he brings out in the king's council

259.reading: Addressed to a woman with coral-red lips and few sweet words, the verse says that the faults of an angry king whose sceptre is otherwise blameless are laid on the attendants beside him, since no doll is unlike the one who made it.
259.nuance: The counsellors are cast as the maker and the king as the doll, so the king's misdeeds are read as the work of those around him; கொள்வர் may mean they take on the blame or that they take on the king's evil ways. பயிரறு, qualifying பக்கத்தார், is obscure: it may be 'whose calling is cut off' or a corrupt word, and the reading does not rest on it.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no doll that does not resemble the one who made it

story.act: no story; the doll and its maker are the instance

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a king's faults are charged to the counsellors who shaped him

260.reading: Addressed to the lord of the great hills where the marai deer calls its mate, the verse says that for one who has not made many of those around him his eyes, there is no steadying when distress comes, like a gourd-lute whose strings are cut.
260.nuance: The lute is still there when the strings are cut, but it can give no sound: the man without counsellors keeps his state but has no response when trouble strikes. The address image, a deer calling its companion, sets beside the counsel a creature that has a mate to call on.

pazhamozhi.literal: it is like cutting the strings of a gourd lute

story.act: no story; the stringless lute is the instance

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a ruler without many counsellors as his eyes is helpless in a crisis

261.reading: The verse says that to seek out by close discussion those who weigh good and ill, grasp what others say and know other good things besides, and then hold them firmly, is as a bull rubs against a bull's back.
261.nuance: The proverb pictures like supporting like: two bulls lean and rub together, each the other's prop. The chooser is not named, but the heading and the testing by கட்டுரை, set speech, point to a king choosing counsellors. வலிப்பது may mean binding them fast or making oneself strong by them; the proverb fits either.

pazhamozhi.literal: the way a bull embraces the back of a bull

story.act: no story; two bulls rubbing together are the instance

pazhamozhi.applied_to: testing the discerning by discussion and holding them close makes them a mutual support

262.reading: The verse describes guardians who are full and subdued in mind, speech, body and every deed, who keep watch in thought and never waver, and says that if there are none such to guard him, life goes and perishes.
262.nuance: The three channels of mind, speech and body, a frame of the Jain and wider ethical codes for restraint, are here demanded of the king's guardians rather than of the ascetic. ஒன்றும் பரியலராய் may mean they are moved by nothing, or that they spare no effort; both make them steadfast. Whose life is at stake is left open; the heading makes it the king's.
262.domain_note: the king's counsellors as his guardians

pazhamozhi.literal: if there are none to guard it, life goes and dies

story.act: no story; an unguarded life is the instance

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a king without restrained, watchful counsellors is lost

263.reading: The verse says that good counsellors make the warring king do the good he does not want to do and stop him when he stands bent on evil, telling him what is for his good even by afflicting him, and so the words of elders are painful at first.
263.nuance: முன் இன்னா, painful first, implies the sweetness after: the elders' counsel is bitter in the hearing and good in its outcome. The counsel works both ways, pushing to unwanted good as well as holding back from evil, and தன்னை நலிந்து admits that the minister's duty is to hurt the king.

pazhamozhi.literal: the word from the mouth of elders is painful at first

story.act: no story; the elders' bitter counsel is the instance

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a good minister's counsel pains the king before it profits him

264.reading: The verse says that when the wise find the garlanded king in a favourable mood they will even use guile, as mothers soothe their children with idle talk of the moon, and closes with the proverb that it is hard for those who show bright things.
264.nuance: The counsellor is likened to a mother who points to the moon to quiet a child, steering by a pleasing show rather than by plain speech; அவ்வியம், usually crookedness or envy, is here a tactful deceit. The proverb as quoted is hard to construe: it may mean that what bright show achieves is hard for others to achieve, or that the moon shown is hard to give. செவ்வியல பெற்றால் may instead be 'if they get the right moments'.

pazhamozhi.literal: it is hard for those who show bright things

story.act: mothers beguile their children with empty talk, pointing to the moon

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the wise may steer a king by artful indirection when his mood allows

265.reading: The verse says that those who know the court's ways do not think of anything that would anger the mighty king even when what he does is not evil, for there is no escape for the deer before the leaping tiger, and likewise no load of straw before the wind.
265.nuance: The proverb is doubled, tiger before deer and wind before straw, both images of a force nothing stands against. தீயன அல்ல செயினும் most likely means even when the king does no wrong, so the caution is not a response to his faults but a standing rule; it could also be read as 'even if he does things other than evil'. சிந்தியார், they do not even think it, puts the restraint in the mind as well as the mouth.

pazhamozhi.proverb: புலிமுன்னர் புல்வாய்க்குப் போக்கில் அதுவே வளிமுன்னர் வைப்பாரம் இல்
pazhamozhi.literal: the deer has no escape before the tiger; just so, a load of straw has none before the wind

story.act: no story; the deer before the tiger and straw before the wind are the instances

pazhamozhi.applied_to: no servant survives the anger of a strong king, so the wise never provoke it

links.note: Kural 717 says the learning of the learned shines among those who can examine words faultlessly; Pazhamozhi 258 says the fierce king's council shows a counsellor's breadth of learning as the flood shows the mountain's rain.
links.teaches: Together they make the assembly a gauge as well as a stage: the Kural needs fit judges for learning to shine, and the Pazhamozhi adds that what pours out there is the measure of what was stored unseen.
links.list_adds: its flood-and-rain proverb turns the couplet's claim about where learning shines into an inference from visible effect to hidden quantity, and sets it in a king's dangerous court.

links.note: Kural 638 makes it the duty of the one at the king's side to tell him his good even when he destroys counsel; Pazhamozhi 259 says the king's faults are laid on those beside him, since no doll is unlike its maker.
links.teaches: The pair gives the duty of plain counsel its sanction: because the world reads the king as his counsellors' making, the one who stays silent shares the guilt of what the king does.
links.list_adds: its doll-and-maker proverb adds the consequence the couplet leaves unsaid, that blame for the king's wrongs passes to his attendants.

links.note: Kural 445 says counsellors are the ruler's eyes and must be chosen with care; Pazhamozhi 260 says one who has not made many around him his eyes is helpless in distress like a lute with cut strings.
links.teaches: Read together, the eyes the Kural asks a ruler to choose are shown at the moment they are missing: in a crisis the king without them still has his state but can make no response, as a stringless lute keeps its body and loses its sound.
links.list_adds: it adds the number, many rather than one, and the crisis in which the lack is felt, with an image of form left without function.

links.note: Kural 441 bids one weigh their worth and take the friendship of the wise who know virtue; Pazhamozhi 261 says to test by discussion those who weigh good and ill and hold them firm, as bull rubs against bull.
links.teaches: The pair names the means of the Kural's weighing, testing in set speech, and its fruit, a support that runs both ways as two bulls prop each other.
links.list_adds: its bull proverb makes the tie between chooser and chosen mutual, where the couplet speaks only of what the chooser gains.

links.note: Kural 442 bids one cherish those who can remove present affliction and guard against what has not come; Pazhamozhi 262 describes guardians restrained in mind, speech and body and says without them life perishes.
links.teaches: Together they show that the Kural's guarding helpers are, for the Pazhamozhi, first of all men disciplined in all three channels, so the ascetic's threefold restraint becomes the qualification of the king's protectors.
links.list_adds: it sets the guardians' power beside their threefold self-restraint as its ground and closes with the stark cost of lacking them.

links.note: Naladiyar 73 asks whether the harsh words of those who love are worse than strangers' smiling sweet words; Pazhamozhi 263 says good ministers press unwanted good on the king and check his evil, so elders' words are painful at first.
links.teaches: The pair carries the friend's welcome harshness up to the throne and adds time: the bitter word is painful only at first, and the minister must also push the king toward good he resists, not only rebuke.
links.list_adds: it moves the claim from friends to minister and king, adds the forward push to unwanted good beside the check on evil, and gives the time-order of pain then profit.

links.note: Kural 448 says a ruler without the guard of those who rebuke perishes even with no enemy; Pazhamozhi 263 says the elders' counsel that saves him is painful at first.
links.teaches: The pair names the cost of the Kural's safeguard: the rebuke that keeps the king from ruin must be borne as pain before it is known as protection, which is why kings are tempted to do without it.
links.list_adds: it adds the cost to the hearer, painful first, which the couplet's plain statement of necessity leaves out.

links.note: Kural 696 bids one know the king's mood and the time and say what is needed and not disliked; Pazhamozhi 264 says the wise, finding the king's favourable moment, will even use guile, as mothers soothe children with the moon.
links.teaches: Together they show how far reading the king's mood can go: the Kural stops at saying the welcome needful thing, while the Pazhamozhi lets the counsellor treat the king as a child to be steered by a pleasing deception.
links.list_adds: its mother-and-moon image adds deceit to the couplet's tact and casts the king as a child, a ranking of counsellor over king the couplet avoids.

links.note: Kural 691 says those who serve quarrelsome kings should be like men warming at a fire, neither too far nor too near; Pazhamozhi 265 says the experienced never even think of what would anger the mighty king, for nothing escapes his force.
links.teaches: The pair shows the fire's danger from inside the servant's mind: the Kural regulates distance, and the Pazhamozhi says the only safety is never to give the king's anger cause, even when he is in the right.
links.list_adds: its doubled proverb of deer before tiger and straw before wind adds that once the king's anger rises there is no escape at any distance, so the caution moves from posture to thought.

links.note: Pazhamozhi 263 praises ministers who afflict the king to tell him his good and stop his evil; Pazhamozhi 265, in the same heading, says the experienced never think of anything that would anger him.
links.teaches: Side by side the two verses of one heading leave the counsellor between duty and survival: the good minister must hurt the king to save him, yet the king's anger is a tiger no one escapes, so the heading gives no single rule.

source_issues: 265 line 4: the closing quotation mark is missing; the proverb is taken to run from புலிமுன்னர் to the end of the verse, and the quotation may have been meant to cover only the second image.
264 line 4: the quotation opens at ஒள்ளிய, after அம்புலிமேல், and the quoted words are hard to construe alone; the placement of the mark is doubtful.
259 line 2: பயிரறு is obscure and may be corrupt.
